items.title: Dan Morgenstern — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: My predecessors were, first, Nat Hentoff, who after all is an old mentor of mine.

ctx.x: . . . pantheon, which has, until about five years ago, only consisted of musicians. But they decided to add a category called “jazz advocate,” which is named for A. B. Spellman, who just retired about a year ago from his 30 years at NEA in the jazz program there. My predecessors were, first, Nat Hentoff, who after all is an old mentor of mine. Then it was George Wein, who we don’t need to say – everybody knows who George was. I intersected with George too. It was George who made it possible for us to bring Art…
Thank you for being present for the easiest interview I’ve ever had to conduct.

items.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013
items.q: Nat Hentoff was also in it.

ctx.x: It helped inform their choices of what to play, yeah, sure. It made them sound more informed.

And actually, one of the reasons why I did that, although I didn’t start initially, was that I’ve done quite a lot of radio over time. I started out at WBAI in New York. And Gunther Schuller and Martin Williams had a program called “The Scope of Jazz.” And Martin had to bow out and he turned it over to me. And so, that was back in the sixties. Nat Hentoff was also in it. Gunther was the first one and then he moved to Boston. Anyway, it was

like a series, one hour jazz, a Sunday night broadcast. But then once I got with the Institute we started, when WBGO was the new jazz radio station in Newark back thirty- some years ago, they came to us at the Institute and asked us to do a weekly program, and we decided to call it “Jazz from the Archives.” And so Ed Berger and Vincent Pelote and I and some of the other people who worked for us would take turns doing the program. We started out, the station didn’t have very much. They had no record library. We of…

items.title: Hentoff Nat — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Yeah, there was some camaraderie. Marshall Stearns was part of that scene, come to think of it. Eventually Dan Morgenstern and all that.

ctx.x: Let’s talk about your peers as a writer in the early 1950s. Was there a sense of community with – eventually, when people came to New York, like Martin Williams and/or the others – Whitney Balliett, these people who you had historic collaborations with?

Yeah. Once I read Martin, I knew I was in the presence of somebody I had to learn from. Same thing with Whitney: nobody was ever able to put the music into words without being precious or self-exalted, etc., and he also had very good ears. I liked him. He was – both – Martin, and there was a guy named Hsio Wen Shih who wrote very well historically. Yeah, there was some camaraderie. Marshall Stearns was part of that scene, come to think of it. Eventually Dan Morgenstern and all that. Yeah, there was a lot of that.
So you’re saying that it’s the Village Voice column is when you began to expand your written topics outside of just jazz music.
